Article Title: In 2020, Minnesota funded a $1.918 million Shell Rock River habitat program; by 2025, it had protected or restored 588 acres
Article Text:
Shell Rock River Watershed District (Image Credit: www.shellrock.org)

A habitat program takes shape

Three properties protected

Wetlands and prairie restored

More acres than planned

A longer-term conservation effort

In 2020, Minnesota approved $1.918 million for the Shell Rock River Watershed Habitat Restoration Program - Phase IX. According to a 2025 final report from the Lessard-Sams Outdoor Heritage Council, the program ultimately protected, restored or enhanced 588 acres of habitat in the Shell Rock River watershed, exceeding its original goal of 483 acres.The funding was provided under Minnesota Laws 2020, with the appropriation directed to the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources for an agreement with the Shell Rock River Watershed District. The funding was intended to support land acquisition as well as the restoration and enhancement of aquatic habitat within the watershed. The program focused on several types of conservation work, including acquiring properties, restoring wetlands and improving aquatic habitat. The projects were selected using conservation planning and monitoring intended to identify areas where habitat improvements could provide significant benefits.The Shell Rock River Watershed is a shallow-lake system that supports fish, waterfowl and other wildlife. According to the final report, restoration projects were targeted at addressing habitat degradation and improving conditions for native fish, waterfowl and wildlife.One part of Phase IX involved acquiring three properties: the Glenville Property, the Bancroft Property, and the Church Lake Property. The District closed on the Glenville Property in March 2021 and the Bancroft Property in September 2021. For the Church Lake Property, the District transferred the deed to the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources in December 2024 after acquiring and restoring the parcel.The final report says these acquisitions contributed to the program's permanent protection of 218 acres. Another 370 acres of habitat and wetlands were enhanced or restored through the program. Together, those accomplishments contributed to the reported total of 588 acres protected, enhanced or restored.The program included several restoration projects beyond property acquisition. The Bancroft Wetland Restoration was initiated in 2020, with construction beginning in June 2024 and largely completed by the fall of that year. Additional seeding work was completed in spring 2025. Another project focused on Panicum Prairie, where habitat enhancement work was carried out across 300 acres. The project involved native prairie vegetation and was substantially completed in February 2025, with final work completed in May.The program also supported the Fountain Lake In-Lake Habitat Project. Work included additional rock reefs and rock boulder clusters intended to improve fish habitat. The report notes that Phase IX funds were used to expand the scope of this work after the District determined additional funds were available. These projects addressed different parts of the watershed's ecosystem, from wetlands and prairie habitat to aquatic areas. The broader aim was to improve habitat conditions while protecting areas that could provide long-term benefits for wildlife.The program's original accomplishment plan called for 483 acres. By the end of the project, the final total had reached 588 acres, 105 acres more than initially planned. The report attributes the increase to the addition of the In-Lake Habitat Project and the Church Lake Property to Phase IX.According to the report, all grant funds were spent. The final grant expenditure remained $1.918 million, while the program's final total including leverage was $1.9479 million.The work is intended to continue beyond the end of the grant. The Shell Rock River Watershed District relies on multiple funding sources, including a local option sales tax, local levy and public funding, to maintain conservation projects. The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources will also maintain the Church Lake Property, which it owns.The program's results illustrate how a single state-funded conservation effort can combine land protection, wetland restoration, prairie enhancement and aquatic habitat improvements. Rather than focusing on one habitat type, Phase IX combined several projects across the Shell Rock River watershed. By 2025, the program had moved beyond its original target, with the final report recording 588 acres protected, enhanced or restored. The completed work represents a combination of permanent land protection and habitat improvements designed to support Minnesota's fish, waterfowl and wildlife over the long term.
Article Summary: In 2020, Minnesota approved $1.918 million for the Shell Rock River Watershed Habitat Restoration Program - Phase IX. By 2025, the program had moved beyond its original target, with the final report recording 588 acres protected, enhanced or restored.

Article Title: America’s top VC Chamath Palihapitiya may have just told Sam Altman and Dario Amodei: You have failed miserably; lists three ‘biggest mistakes’
Article Text:
Political fallout in the Ohio Senate race

Chamath Palihapitiya points to three things that are needed

Chamath Palihapitiya, a prominent venture capitalist and “All-In Podcast” co-host, has issued a warning to the leaders of top artificial intelligence (AI) labs, arguing that the technology sector is currently sitting on a dangerous ‘powder keg’ caused by mounting public and political opposition to physical data centres. According to Palihapitiya, the executive leadership leading cutting-edge AI development has failed to persuade citizens of the sector's merits and the community-level value of hosting infrastructure facilities.“Data centers have unfortunately become THE symbolic representation of the asymmetric upside for a very narrow tech elite and a class that are untrustworthy,” Palihapitiya said in a post on X (formerly Twitter).Palihapitiya’s remarks came as a direct reaction to reporting from Axios revealing that the campaign branch for Senate Republicans sent a stern memo to prominent AI development organizations. The communication from the National Republican Senatorial Committee pointed out that data centres have turned into a fierce campaign vulnerability in Ohio, where former Senator Sherrod Brown is competing in a tight race against Republican incumbent Senator Jon Husted.Husted is running to complete the remainder of Vice President JD Vance's term.“Texas, Pennsylvania and now Ohio. This is a powder keg and has the potential to unwind 200-300 basis points of annual GDP if it metastasizes. How did it get this bad? The collective leadership of frontier AI has failed miserably in doing the basics,” he added.The committee noted that the two candidates are locked in a dead heat, warning that data centers represent the heaviest anchor dragging down Husted's campaign.To repair the widening trust deficit, Palihapitiya advised industry figures to end internal conflicts and adopt an uplifting, accessible public message rather than relying on technical jargon or stoking doomsday scenarios.1. Paint a positive picture of what is possible with AI. Instead of spilling the ink on the glass half full, stories abound of pearl clutching, catastrophizing or arcane technical jargon that, together, breed mistrust, fear and skepticism.2. Visibly and disproportionately enrich the local communities AI data centers operate in. Tell these stories with a megaphone and have local leaders lead with the financial proof so it’s irrefutable.3. Stop infighting and stop trying to influence the government or trick them because of the asymmetric knowledge the industry has relative to outsiders and observers. This further makes it seem like a shady money grab to many bystanders.He stressed that companies must clearly demonstrate the positive everyday possibilities enabled by AI.
Article Summary: Venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya says AI sector is sitting on a dangerous 'powder keg' He points to mounting public and political opposition to physical data centres. He advises industry figures to end internal conflicts and adopt an uplifting, accessible public message.

Article Title: Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra's 'reminder' to everyone investing in AI and calling it 'big': Right now, there is no AI without ...
Article Text:
Micron CEO feels AI is creating a more durable source

Demand outstripping supply

US chipmaker Micron reaches $1 trillion market capitalization

Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra recently said that artificial intelligence has fundamentally transformed the memory industry, long known for its boom-and-dust cycles. “Today there is no AI without memory. AI systems need more memory. They need higher performance memory. They need lower power memory,” Mehrotra told CNBC’s Jim Cramer on Mad Money. “So, the value of memory, that equation has totally changed.” His remarks came as Micron builds a vast semiconductor fabrication site near its Boise, Idaho headquarters, part of a planned $250 billion investment in U.S. manufacturing and research. The Boise complex will eventually house two fabs, each the size of 10 football fields, with the first expected to begin wafer production in mid‑2027.Mehrotra, who co‑founded SanDisk and has worked in chips for over 40 years, said AI is creating a more durable source of demand across data centers, autonomous vehicles, robots, and consumer devices. “Memory today is essential. That’s why I call it the strategic infrastructure of the AI era,” he said.Micron still cannot produce enough to meet demand. Mehrotra said data‑center customers want about 50% more supply than Micron can commit.The company has signed five‑year strategic agreements with 16 customers, with more added since its June earnings call, giving it greater visibility into long‑term demand. “All our customers across our end markets will buy everything that we make,” he said.In related news, recently, US chipmaker Micron Technology briefly crossed a market value of $1 trillion on May 26 as investor excitement around AI continued to drive demand for memory chips. According to a report by news agency Reuters, the sharp rally made Micron one of the biggest winners of the AI boom, with its shares rising more than 17% during trading. Micron’s stock jumped after brokerage UBS raised its price target on the company to $1,625 from $535, the report said. The company’s shares rose as much as 19.3% during the session before easing slightly later.As cited in the Reuters report, analysts say the surge reflects growing demand for advanced memory chips used in AI data centers and cloud infrastructure. The company’s rise also highlights how investors are now focusing beyond graphics chipmakers and looking at firms supplying key AI hardware components. “The need for pure memory has increased rapidly over very short periods of time, and clearly, Micron sits at the center of it,” Art Hogan, chief market strategist at B. Riley Wealth, told Reuters. “Today's crossing of the $1 trillion mark for Micron is just an exclamation point on the story of the massive amount of demand needed to run data centers in this AI revolution,” he added.
Article Summary: US chipmaker Micron reaches $1 trillion market capitalization. CEO Sanjay Mehrotra says AI is creating a more durable source of demand. Micron still cannot produce enough to meet demand for memory chips, MehroTra says. The company has signed five‑year strategic agreements with 16 customers.

Article Title: Mark Zuckerberg buys Gothic castle in Ireland, Meta's international headquarters, for $35 million
Article Text:
Mark Zuckerberg's Ireland home

Why Mark Zuckerberg bought the castle

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and wife Priscilla Chan have bought Strancally Castle, a Gothic-style mansion in Ireland, for an estimated $35 million, according to reports. The historic property sits on a 178-hectare (440-acre) estate in County Waterford and will serve as a base for the couple when they visit Ireland. The purchase also has a connection to Meta, which maintains its international headquarters in Ireland. A Meta spokesperson said Mark Zuckerberg and his family are looking forward to caring for the historic property and spending time in the country.The exact amount paid for the castle has not been made public. The Irish Times estimated its value at between €20 million and €30 million.Strancally Castle was built in 1830 for John Keily, a former Conservative MP. Architects James and George Richard Pain designed the property on a large scale. The castle is part of a 440-acre estate in County Waterford. According to the book The Houses of Ireland, the size of the property was such that it once took a few minutes to walk from the dining room to the kitchen.The property was bought and renovated in the early 2000s by Michael Alen-Buckley, co-founder of investment firm RAB Capital, and his wife, Giancarla.The couple said they were pleased that Zuckerberg and his family planned to continue maintaining the property.Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan are expected to use Strancally Castle as their base when visiting Ireland. The purchase also comes as Meta maintains its international headquarters in Ireland, making the country an important location for the company.“Mark and his family are excited to continue caring for this historic home and look forward to spending time in Ireland, where Meta maintains its international headquarters,” a Meta spokesperson was quoted as saying.Strancally Castle is located in the Blackwater Valley, an area known for historic estates. The National Built Heritage Service, an Irish state agency, describes the castle as having sandstone and limestone construction and highlights its stonework and craftsmanship.“The construction in sandstone and limestone ashlar augments the dour tone of the composition while providing evidence of high quality stone masonry and craftsmanship,” it says.The area is also home to other properties owned by wealthy business figures. Entrepreneur James Dyson bought Ballynatray House in 2024, while Stripe co-founder John Collison bought Abbey Leix in County Laois in 2021.
Article Summary: Strancally Castle was built in 1830 for John Keily, a former Conservative MP. The castle is part of a 440-acre estate in County Waterford. The exact amount paid for the castle has not been made public. The purchase also has a connection to Meta, which maintains its international headquarters in Ireland.

Article Title: IBM CEO Arvind Krishna on his letter that ‘shocked’ business world, sent company's stock over 25 percent down, making it 'worst day' in IBM history
Article Text:
IBM CEO Arvind Krishna

Why IBM CEO thinks it was important to ‘tell’ beforehand

Facing an impending quarterly earnings miss driven by shifting enterprise IT budgets and rising AI distractions, IBM Chairman and CEO Arvind Krishna opted for radical transparency -- a move that triggered a historic stock plunge but is reported to have aligned with his core leadership philosophy. In an interview with CRN, IBM CEO Krishna detailed the high-stakes decision to pre-announce the 115-year-old tech giant's financial shortfall eight days before its scheduled July 22 earnings call. The disclosure sent IBM shares tumbling more than 25%, marking one of the steepest single-day declines in the company's history.IBM's underperformance stemmed from enterprise clients pausing infrastructure projects to front-load spending on data center hardware amid supply constraints and surging costs. Additionally, Krishna noted that customer attention had been diverted by security debates surrounding an AI model released by Anthropic. He reduced IBM's expected full-year revenue growth for the year by more than $600 million, saying that the fall is in part due to some clients pushing out IBM infrastructure projects to pay for the growing cost of supply constrained memory, storage, servers and other data center infrastructure.Rather than holding the bad news for the standard earnings cycle, Krishna fell back on a long-standing operating principle: "If there’s a hard thing to be done, do it earlier rather than later," Krishna told CRN.By clearing the bad news early, Krishna aimed to pivot the official earnings call away from post-mortem explanations and toward strategic fixes. "Time will tell whether that was the right decision. I tend to think it was," Krishna said. "Otherwise, we would have been spending the last week explaining the hesitation as opposed to what we are going to do to go fix it."The decision highlights the pressures facing IBM as it balances heavy investments in generative AI and long-term quantum computing against Wall Street's short-term expectations. When asked by CRN about potential vulnerability to activist investors or board friction following the market reaction, the CEO, who took the helm in April 2020, remained pragmatic about corporate oversight."If you falter, one should always be just prepared is my view," Krishna said, adding that public CEOs must constantly evaluate whether they are delivering sufficient returns. "And activists, at the end, if I look at the good side, are trying to come in to say, 'I need better returns for clients and for investors.' And if that’s the goal, then one should be prepared to deal with them. That is just the nature of today’s world that we live in. "Krishna maintained that his primary strategy to protect the company's innovation roadmap remains centered on client satisfaction and workforce investment.IBM CEO Krishna reasoned the Q2 weakness to deal ‘deferral, and not destruction’. He said, “This was deferral and not destruction.” Krishna made the statement while talking to analysts during IBM’s latest quarterly earnings call with analysts. Krishna’s confidence comes in part from the fact that one-third of those largest infrastructure projects requiring a lot of customer CapEx have already closed.
Article Summary: IBM Chairman and CEO Arvind Krishna opted for radical transparency. The disclosure sent IBM shares tumbling more than 25%, marking one of the steepest single-day declines in the company's history. Krishna: "If there’s a hard thing to be done, do it earlier rather than later"

Article Title: Elon Musk’s Starlink seeks fresh India approval; says it will help ‘least served’...
Article Text:
What Elon Musk said about Starlink’s India launch

Starlink’s second attempt after an earlier rejection

Direct‑to‑device tech imminent

Regulatory and security challenges

Elon Musk’s Starlink has renewed efforts to launch satellite communication services in India. According to a report by Economic Times, the company is resubmitting an application to the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN‑SPACe) for approval of its Gen 2 constellation. The new system would operate at altitudes of 340–615 km in low earth orbit and introduce direct‑to‑device (D2D) connectivity, a feature Musk has touted as critical for reaching underserved communities.Elon Musk underscored the importance of Starlink’s India push in a recent post on X, saying the service would help the “least served” communities. Replying to a post on X, Musk wrote, ‘Starlink would help the least served in India, especially in rural areas.’The Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) had rejected an earlier application from the Elon Musk-owned company for its planned 30,000-satellite internet constellation a few years ago, citing non-conformity in certain features and spectrum bands. According to a person familiar with the details, who spoke on condition of anonymity since the specifics aren't public, the company has now applied for authorisation of its Gen 2 constellation, which would operate at an altitude of 340-615 km in low earth orbit.Starlink, operated by SpaceX and the world's largest LEO satellite operator, remains bullish on India's satcom market, which industry watchers describe as still nascent but carrying significant long-term potential. The company had originally applied for both Gen 1 and Gen 2 constellations to begin services in India, but IN-SPACe approved only the Gen 1 constellation, comprising 4,408 LEO satellites offering traditional broadband services, in July 2025.India is considering opening more spectrum bands for satellite communications and allowing D2D features, prompting Starlink’s reapplication. If approved, the Gen 2 constellation could give Starlink a significant edge by enabling mobile connectivity directly to consumer devices, bypassing traditional telecom networks.So far, no non‑geostationary satellite operator — including Starlink, OneWeb, or Jio’s SES joint venture — has launched commercial services in India due to pending security clearances and spectrum allocation. The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has issued pricing recommendations, but the government has yet to finalize rules. Telecom operators have warned that D2D services could threaten their business and have pushed for satellite firms to face the same regulatory obligations.
Article Summary: Starlink has renewed efforts to launch satellite communication services in India. The company is resubmitting an application to the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN‑SPACe) for approval of its Gen 2 constellation. The new system would operate at altitudes of 340–615 km in low earth orbit and introduce direct‑to‑device (D2D) connectivity.

Article Title: Apple Music Apple Music follows Spotify, to start labelling AI-generated music
Article Text: Apple Music will begin labelling songs created with artificial intelligence later this year, according to an email sent to industry partners and obtained by The Hollywood Reporter. The streaming service said that AI Transparency Tags will be required whenever AI is used to generate a material portion of a track including those primary divided from generative AI platforms.The move builds on Apple Music’s introduction of transparency tags in March, which allowed record labels and distributors to disclose AI‑generated content during uploads. With the new policy, those tags will become visible to listeners, making AI involvement in tracks clear. Apple Music did not specify how enforcement will work.The announcement follows calls from the RIAA and IFPI for streaming platforms to adopt AI labels similar to explicit content disclosures. Apple joins Spotify, which earlier this month said it would label AI artists on the platform, though Spotify’s system applies to artist profiles rather than individual tracks.Apple Music has already taken steps to combat streaming fraud, doubling penalty fees in January. Head of Apple Music Oliver Schusser previously acknowledged that AI proliferation was a factor, noting that while over a third of monthly uploads are AI‑generated, actual usage of AI songs remains below 1%.
Article Summary: AI Transparency Tags will be required whenever AI is used to generate a material portion of a track. Apple joins Spotify, which earlier this month said it would label AI artists on the platform. Apple Music has already taken steps to combat streaming fraud, doubling penalty fees in January.

Article Title: Iran war risk: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warns of oil shocks, sticky inflation and higher interest rates
Article Text: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has warned that the ongoing war in Iran could trigger oil and commodity price shocks, keeping inflation elevated and pushing interest rates higher than current market expectations, Reuters reported.The warning came in his annual letter to shareholders, a day after US President Donald Trump escalated pressure on Iran by threatening to target key infrastructure if the Strait of Hormuz is not reopened."Now, because of the war in Iran, we additionally face the potential for significant ongoing oil and commodity price shocks, along with the reshaping of global supply chains, which may lead to stickier inflation and ultimately higher interest rates than markets currently expect," Dimon said, news agency Reuters quoted as saying.Dimon, who has led JPMorgan for two decades, also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China."The challenges we all face are significant," he added.He said it remains uncertain whether the Iran war will achieve US objectives, while warning that nuclear proliferation remains the biggest risk linked to Iran.Markets have already begun pricing in these risks, with expectations of interest rate cuts this year largely fading amid rising inflation concerns triggered by the conflict.Last week, the benchmark S&P 500 index recorded its worst quarterly performance since 2022, weighed down by rising energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty since late February.Dimon noted that the US economy remains resilient, with consumers continuing to earn and spend, and businesses staying broadly healthy, though signs of weakening have emerged.He cautioned that economic strength has been supported by significant government deficit spending and past stimulus, while infrastructure investment needs continue to grow.At the same time, he pointed to positives such as fiscal stimulus under President Trump's "Big, Beautiful Bill", deregulation policies and rising capital expenditure driven by artificial intelligence.On financial stability, Dimon said the $1.8-trillion private credit market "probably" does not pose a systemic risk, despite investor concerns and recent withdrawals from such funds.However, he warned that in a downturn, losses across leveraged lending could exceed expectations as credit standards have weakened.Private credit markets also lack transparency and rigorous valuation benchmarks, increasing the risk of investor exits if conditions worsen, he said.Separately, Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical" and "very flawed".He said JPMorgan’s GSIB surcharge would fall only to 5.0%, a level he described as “absurd” and “un-American”, arguing it penalises the bank’s scale and performance.
Article Summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warns Iran war could trigger oil and commodity price shocks. He also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China. Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical"

Article Title: How selling Alaska in 1867 was a costly mistake for Russia
Article Text:
Image: Wikipedia

Why Russia agreed to the Alaska purchase

The hidden wealth Russia gave away

Strategic and geopolitical consequences







In 1867, Russia’s decision to sell Alaska to America turned out to be a historic mistake that was to go unnoticed for years to come. The sum paid by the US was only $7,200,000. Although, in the light of the circumstances at the time, it appeared logical, retrospectively, the act looks extremely shortsighted. Russia found itself economically constrained, geographically far away from the region and fearful of its falling into the hands of the British without any compensation. In reality, however, the region had proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Its vast reserves of oil, gold, and natural resources would later transform it into one of the most economically significant territories in the United States.The choice of selling Alaska was based on economic and political reasons. By the middle of the 19th century, the Russian Empire experienced financial difficulties as a result of the expensive Crimean War. It had become increasingly hard for the country to manage such remote and thinly populated areas as Alaska.According to EBSCO , “the Russian-American Company was in decline, and the colony failed to yield any profit”.In addition to this, the lucrative fur trade had declined, making the territory much less economically valuable for the empire.At the same time, Russia was afraid that Britain might capture Alaska in case another war broke out between the two countries. Selling the colony to the friendly United States appeared as a logical step. As the Office of the Historian states, William H. Seward, U.S. Secretary of State, “it was a chance to expand its influence in North America and hinder further growth of Britain”.For Russia, the transaction was a chance to minimise the losses. However, it greatly undervalued the potential of Alaska.Another thing that Russia did not expect was the amount of riches that Alaska possessed. Within several decades after the acquisition, the state saw discoveries of enormous deposits of gold, oil, and other minerals.“Alaska has produced more than 40 million ounces of gold,” according to the US Geological Survey. Furthermore, Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) . But even more importantly, the state's oil deposits turned out to be extremely valuable. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968 and became one of North America's biggest.In retrospect, the amount paid by the Americans, $7.2 million, or two cents per acre, was rather laughable. According to Howard I. Kushner , the deal “robbed Russia of an enormously rich territory, the true value of which would only be recognised in the twentieth century.”In addition to resources, there is the question of strategy and how important Alaska is to the United States from a strategic standpoint. This is a very good place when it comes to defence strategy. It borders on the Arctic Ocean and also happens to be close to Russia.During the period of the Cold War, the Alaskan region became a frontier area for the United States, becoming home to military facilities and warning systems.According to Col. Michael J. Forsyth, U.S. Army, the closeness of Russia and Alaska, only about ninety kilometres apart across the Bering Strait, meant that this region became highly significant to the United States' defence plans.From today's point of view, the strategic location of Alaska makes the state very important to the policies of the U.S. related to the Arctic, energy security, and even environmental policies.Thinking back, what seems clear to us now is that the Russians sold Alaska due to immediate needs rather than future considerations. In order to solve the problem, they lost a valuable resource for Russia.Conclusively, the Alaska Purchase should not have been done as it has had a significant impact that will remain throughout history.
Article Summary: Russia sold Alaska to the U.S. in 1867 for only $7,200,000. The sale was based on economic and political reasons. However, the region proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968.

Article Title: AI data centers are causing 'stress' not just to tech companies, but also private insurers
Article Text:
Massive investments, growing risks



Unique challenges for data centre insurance companies





AI data centers are reportedly putting new pressure on the insurance industry. According to a CNBC report, experts warn that the rapid growth of these projects is becoming a “stress test” not just for tech companies, but also for private insurers and lenders. Consulting firm McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. As costs rise, tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects. The scale of investments is creating challenges for insurers.“When you put $10 to $20 billion plus in a single location, it creates capacity issues in the marketplace,” said Tom Harper, data center leader at insurance broker Gallagher as quoted in the CNBC report.He added that the sector has been a “real stress test” over the last few years, as insurers struggle to provide coverage for such large and complex projects. While these facilities are seen as high-quality assets, Harper said insuring them has become difficult due to their size and risk concentration.Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Companies including Nvidia, Microsoft and BlackRock have already taken part in large investment deals.Rajat Rana, partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, described the scale as unprecedented. “We’re talking about trillions of dollars, and almost going back to the same cycle where there’s almost no transparency about the financing structures — the scale is astronomical,” he said. He added that the boom in AI data centers could be “the largest peacetime investment project in human history.”Experts say the way these projects are financed is adding another layer of risk. Much of the funding is happening through complex and less transparent debt structures. Rana warned that this trend feels like “deja vu,” referring to past financial cycles. He said the lack of transparency could create risks for investors, insurers and pension funds.As stated in the CNBC report, data centers offer unique challenges due to their mix of real estate and advanced technology. Insurers are now designing custom policies to manage these risks. However, challenges remain. Large facilities are often located in areas prone to extreme weather, and they store expensive equipment, sometimes even before installation.Another key concern is the mismatch between the lifespan of data centers and the hardware they use. While data centers can last decades, GPUs — the chips powering AI — typically last around seven years. Rana described this as a “GPU debt treadmill,” saying, “This is almost like a treadmill that these AI data centers are running on.”He explained that companies may need to keep raising debt to upgrade infrastructure as technology evolves.
Article Summary: Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. Tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects.

Article Title: DU opens direct PhD path for this year's FYUP grads
Article Text:
Delhi University will offer direct PhD admissions for the 2026-27 academic session.

TOI

TOI





NEW DELHI: Delhi University has announced a direct admission route to PhD programmes as a one-time measure for those who completed the four-year undergraduate programme this year, reports Sugandha Jha.In a press release issued Friday, DU said, "In the interest of the first batch of students who have completed the FYUP in 2026, the university will admit students who have 7.5 CGPA (7 CGPA for SC/ST) and above in the FYUP directly to the PhD programme, only for the academic session 2026-27, as a special measure as per rules of the university."DU Registrar Vikas Gupta toldthat those who are eligible will have to sit for an entrance test, dates for which will be announced soon. Aspirants will not be required to appear for an interview.Gupta added that the relaxation was limited to the first batch of FYUP students, given the teething issues faced by the inaugural batch. “This will not be applicable for upcoming batches. The modalities will be decided later if the same has to be rolled out for other batches later,” he said. The university has also amended its PhD ordinance to enable FYUP graduates meeting the prescribed criteria to apply directly for doctoral programmes.The decision was taken in a meeting of the university’s executive council on July 30. Gupta said it followed reports of confusion and challenges surrounding the implementation of the new system for the first FYUP batch.The decision, however, faced objections by some executive council members who said the proposal was not thorough and could cause difficulties for students. For example, if a student applies for a teaching position, she requires a master’s degree. If FYUP students choose to go for the PhD programme, they may have to do a master’s degree after. Similarly, students who go through this route will not be able to give the NET exam since a postgraduate degree is an eligibility criteria. They also said admitting students to PhD programmes without any interview would mean that there is no credible method to ensure that the student’s research is academically viable and valid, as per PhD standards.had reported Friday that FYUP graduates across universities, including DU, were entering an academic vacuum, as a limited number of one-year PG programmes was forcing many students to take up the traditional two-year masters’ degree and that the proposal to allow direct admission to PhD programmes was yet to take off.The university said 75,948 students took admission in the FYUP in 2022-23. Of them, 40,005 exited after the third year in 2025. The university said FYUP was designed to bring research and entrepreneurship into undergraduate education and align Indian degrees with global standards.
Article Summary: Delhi University will offer direct PhD admissions for the 2026-27 academic session. Those who are eligible will have to sit for an entrance test. Aspirants will not be required to appear for an interview. The decision was taken in a meeting of the university’s executive council on July 30.

Article Title: Putting regeneration back into textile ecosystem
Article Text:
‘Lot of learning in store for handloom lovers’

Union Minister of Textiles Giriraj Singh interacts with a kani shawl weaver

‘Lot of learning in store for handloom lovers'

Giriraj Singh

Dr M Beena,

Dr M Beena, DC (Handlooms) and Neelam Shami Rao, Secretary, Ministry of Textiles

Shubhi Sachan, founder of the Material Library of India, who curated the exhibition

The Visvakarma Gallery is a permanent exhibition showcasing rare textiles from a landmark exhibition series held between 1981 and 1991

David Abraham with Rakesh Thakore

Rajeev Sethi visiting the Visvakarma Gallery

The journey of brown cotton from soil to fabric

Customers take a look at CRCLE's korai grass bag

Leela Ler's fully compostable apparel and Salooka shirt made using HimGra fibre

Clockwise: Tvastri's bamboo craft bag, Parul Gupta's brand Label Yuga's mogra brooch, Pillikothi Home's nettle fabric cushion cover and Kanika Sahijwani's brand Pusaaka's bead bags





What if every garment we wear could be traced back to nature, and at the end of its life, return to it? At a time when fast fashion has made textile consumption increasingly linear and disposable, the installations at Weave the Future 5.0 makes a case for a more regenerative relationship with what we wear.The idea of building a circular relationship with our clothes sets the tone for the fifth edition of Weave the Future, which was inaugurated by Minister of Textilesat Handloom Haat in Janpath last week. This edition expands the conversation around regenerative and circular textile practices, bringing indigenous and emerging fibres into focus.Development Commissioner (Handlooms), said the space brings together weavers, artisans, designers and sustainability champions, while making a case for handloom beyond its traditional positioning. “It is aspirational. The brands are exhibiting innovative materials and fibres which people haven’t heard of. There is a lot of learning and discovery for any handloom lover,” she said.Speaking at the exhibition, Singh said, “Handloom has a naturally lower carbon footprint and immense potential to emerge as a sustainable fabric for fashion, clothing and home décor.” He added that the focus was on strengthening the handloom ecosystem by improving incomes, expanding market access and creating new opportunities for weavers.Alongside the exhibition, visitors got a glimpse of the Handloom Experience Centre, which is the re-envisioned Handloom Haat, celebrating the enduring relevance of India’s handloom sector.The Visvakarma Gallery is a permanent exhibition showcasing rare textiles from a landmark exhibition series held between 1981 and 1991. Developed through collaborations between Weavers’ Service Centres and artisan communities, the collection offers a window into our textile heritage and its evolution in the decades following Independence.Sushma Veerapa showcased the journey of cotton from farm to fibre. About her work at Kandu, she said, "Cotton is valuable when made into a product. So, we collaborated with a farmer growing naturally brown cotton, grown with desi seeds. Now 55 farmers are engaged. To die the brown yarn we are using lily, leaves of wedeliya creeper and indigo."Varshne, founder of CRCLE, who has been working with weganool (nool means thread in Tamil), said, "The point is to ensure nothing gets discarded and everything goes back into production — either into the soil or into the production cycle. Regeneration, for us, also means working with plant-based materials. Weganool is made from the fibre of the calotropis plant. We also work with korai grass, traditionally used to make chattai. We collaborate with artisans to create these mats in specific colours and patterns, which are then transformed into bags."Showing a rust shirt made from Himalayan grass fibre, with chikankari embroidery done using a broken 100-year-old block, Shubhangi Bajpai, founder of Salooka, said, “Regeneration is not just about the anatomy of a textile; it can also be about how we reuse materials, surfaces and processes.”“Regeneration is about discovering new possibilities in indigenous materials, from cardamom fibre to water hyacinth," Hena Dasari from Tvastri, who have been using fibres like banana fibre, sitalpati, madurkathi stalks to make home utility items and bags.“We are exploring the possibilities of indigenous Indian fibres through hand-spun and handwoven textiles, reimagined for contemporary living. From nettle (bicchu booti) and bhimal to mountain wools, it is interesting to work with materials rooted in local landscapes,” said Devica Sud, founder, PilliKothi Home showing a nettle fabric cushion cover with kantha embroidery.
Article Summary: The Visvakarma Gallery is a permanent exhibition showcasing rare textiles from a landmark exhibition series held between 1981 and 1991. The fifth edition of Weave the Future was inaugurated by Minister of Textilesat Handloom Haat in Janpath last week.

Article Title: NGT disposes of plea challenging construction on 95 acres of Bijwasan project land
Article Text: New Delhi: National Green Tribunal has disposed of a plea challenging construction on about 95 acres of land for the Bijwasan rail project in Dwarka, holding that the issue was covered by a March 2026 judgement of the Supreme Court (SC) concerning the same project area.The application filed by Naveen Solanki had raised the issue of whether the 95 acres of land fell within the ambit of “deemed forest” and therefore required protection under the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980. The applicant had alleged that the disputed land was part of a larger 125-acre forest area and that around 13,000 trees were spread over the 95 acres. The applicant had also raised allegations of illegal felling of trees.NGT noted that the 95 acres formed part of a larger 125-acre parcel, of which the remaining 30 acres had already been considered by Tribunal in an earlier case. SC, in its March 20, 2026 judgement, had affirmed the NGT’s earlier order and considered the entire project land.“The Supreme Court has found that the subject land formed part of larger tract of agricultural land acquired in 1986 and allotted for development of Bijwasan Integrated Passenger Terminal and incorporated in Master Plan, 2021.At the time of formulation of Master Plan, the land was not notified as forest or declared as forest or treated as deemed forest,” observed the bench comprising chairperson Justice Prakash Shrivastava and expert member Afroz Ahmad, in an order dated Aug 7.At the same time, the tribunal directed that the safeguards and directions issued by SC would apply to the 95-acre land as well. These include making maximum efforts for transplantation of native/indigenous trees, preservation and protection of existing trees, and undertaking compensatory afforestation before commencement of work.
Article Summary: The application filed by Naveen Solanki had raised the issue of whether the 95 acres of land fell within the ambit of ‘deemed forest’ The applicant had alleged that the disputed land was part of a larger 125-acre forest area. The applicant also raised allegations of illegal felling of trees.

Article Title: Committee of auto, e-rickshaw drivers formed to ease Chhattarpur congestion
Article Text: New Delhi: With heavy pedestrian movement and a constant stream of autos, e-rickshaws and Gramin Seva vehicles choking roads around Chhattarpur Metro station, Delhi Traffic Police has stepped up measures to ease congestion at CDR Chowk and Mandir Wali Road in Mehrauli.DCP (Traffic), Southern Range, inspected the stretch recently and interacted with drivers of public transport vehicles.The inspection found that commuters use the various modes of public transport to travel to and from Chhattarpur metro station, putting pressure on the already congested stretch, particularly during peak hours. Officials also flagged haphazard stopping and parking of autos and e-rickshaws as a major cause of congestion.To bring some order to the situation, a committee comprising representatives of auto- and e-rickshaw drivers has now been formed. The committee will coordinate with drivers and ensure that vehicles are parked strictly in a single line, without blocking the carriageway or pedestrian movement.Traffic Inspector, Mehrauli, and personnel deployed in the area have also been directed to keep a watch on the stretch and take strict enforcement action against vehicles violating parking and traffic norms.
Article Summary: Delhi Traffic Police has stepped up measures to ease congestion at CDR Chowk and Mandir Wali Road in Mehrauli. A committee comprising representatives of auto- and e-rickshaw drivers has now been formed. The committee will coordinate with drivers and ensure that vehicles are parked strictly in a single line, without blocking the carriageway.
